Reference-bias simulations (v2, mason2) — chr19 divergence sweep

gwct

07/30/2026 22:41:59 EDT

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", out.width = "80%")

# Individual tidyverse components (the renv env does not carry the tidyverse
# meta-package). cowplot is used to compose multi-panel figures; design.r
# provides the repo-wide plotting theme (bartheme) and palette (corecol) so
# these v2 figures match the visual style of the v1 docs.
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(cowplot)
source("docs/scripts/lib/design.r")

1 Introduction & methods

This notebook summarizes the v2 (mason2-based) reference-bias simulation for a single chromosome (mouse chr19, mm39). It replaces the v1 (NEAT-based) pipeline, whose read-mapping “truth” required a fragile CrossMap liftover that injected a constant, spurious “missing reads” artifact (~840k–1.4M reads even at zero divergence). In v2 the truth is produced directly in reference coordinates by mason_simulator, so no liftover is needed.

Pipeline (single iteration):

make_truth_vcf.py (controlled truth VCF) → mason_simulator (reads + truth BAM) → bwa mem (map back to chr19) → GATK HaplotypeCaller→GenotypeGVCFs→filter→SNPs → compare_bams.py / compare_vcfs.py → summary tables.

Simulation grid. One chromosome (chr19, length 61,420,004), coverage 30X, heterozygosity fixed at H = 0.5%, divergence D swept over {0.00, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10}, with 3 replicate seeds (42–44). Points/curves show the mean over seeds; error bars, where drawn, are ±1 SD. The sample genome also carries small indels at 1/8 of the SNP rate (indel divergence = D/8, indel heterozygosity = H/8; sizes 1–6 bp, insertions and deletions), so SNP recovery here is measured in the presence of indels.

Key definitions (see the accompanying .dict.txt files for full column docs):

  • Divergence D — fraction of sites made homozygous-alternate (truth GT 1|1); the sample’s fixed differences from the reference.
  • Heterozygosity H — fraction of sites made heterozygous (truth GT 0|1); polymorphism within the diploid sample.
  • Read placement classes (each primary read matched to its truth position by read name; tolerance = one read length, 150 bp): exact (delta 0), close (≤150 bp), mismapped (same contig, >150 bp), unmapped, and missing (in truth but absent from the mapped BAM — the v1 artifact, expected 0 here).
  • Variant-call classes at divergence sites — div_tp (correctly called homozygous-alt), div_het (called heterozygous), div_ref_or_absent (called homozygous-reference OR not called — the reference-bias failure), div_other (wrong allele / multiallelic edge case).
  • Indel call classes — mirror the SNP classes: indel_div_tp (recovered), indel_div_ref_or_absent (reference-bias failure), indel_div_other.
  • Filtering. GATK calls are excluded where MQ < 30 | FORMAT/DP < 5 | FORMAT/DP > 60 | ALT="*", then left-aligned/normalized (bcftools norm); SNPs and indels are compared separately by matching (POS, REF, ALT) against the truth.
# Raw tables have one row per (divergence, seed). We average over the replicate seeds
# for the summary curves, and keep the per-seed tables (bam_raw / vcf_raw) for error bars.
bam_raw <- read_csv("summary-data/mm39-mason-chr19-bam-summary.csv")
vcf_raw <- read_csv("summary-data/mm39-mason-chr19-vcf-summary.csv")

bam <- bam_raw %>% group_by(divergence) %>%
  summarize(across(where(is.numeric), mean), .groups = "drop")
vcf <- vcf_raw %>% group_by(divergence) %>%
  summarize(across(where(is.numeric), mean), .groups = "drop")

n_seeds <- dplyr::n_distinct(vcf_raw$seed)
chr19_len <- 61420004

2 Read mapping accuracy

2.1 Composition of read placements across divergence

The stacked bars show the proportion of reads in each placement class. We separate a whole-read positional shift (fully aligned, moved ≤150 bp) from soft-clipping (divergent read end dropped from the alignment) — mechanistically different, and the clipped class also absorbs 3′-clipped reads that still sit at the exact start position (previously mislabelled “exact”).

read_classes <- c("exact","shifted","clipped","mismapped","diff_chr","unmapped","missing")
read_labels  <- c("Exact","Shifted (moved <=150bp)","Soft-clipped","Mismapped",
                  "Different contig","Unmapped","Missing")

read_long <- bam %>%
  select(divergence, all_of(paste0(read_classes, "_prop"))) %>%
  pivot_longer(-divergence, names_to = "class", values_to = "prop") %>%
  mutate(class = factor(sub("_prop","",class), levels = read_classes))

cols <- corecol(pal = "wilke", numcol = length(read_classes), offset = 1)

ggplot(read_long, aes(x = divergence, y = prop, fill = class)) +
  geom_col(position = position_fill(reverse = TRUE), width = 0.015) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(read_long$divergence)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols, labels = read_labels) +
  xlab("Simulated divergence (D)") + ylab("Proportion of reads") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

2.2 Non-exact placements: clipping dominates

Isolating the non-exact classes shows the mechanism clearly: soft-clipping grows explosively with divergence (0.6% → 62% of reads at D=0.10), while a whole-read positional shift stays negligible (~2%). Mismapping rises only gently, unmapped dropout appears only at 8–10%, and missing is exactly zero throughout (the v1 liftover artifact is gone).

err_long <- read_long %>% filter(class %in% c("shifted","clipped","mismapped","unmapped"))
ecols <- c("shifted"="#56b4e9","clipped"="#e69f00","mismapped"="#d55e00","unmapped"="#000000")

ggplot(err_long, aes(x = divergence, y = prop, color = class)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2) + geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(err_long$divergence)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = ecols,
                     labels = c("Shifted","Soft-clipped","Mismapped","Unmapped")) +
  xlab("Simulated divergence (D)") + ylab("Proportion of reads") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Interpretation. Reads almost always land at the right locus (mismapping stays <2%, and true unmapped dropout appears only at the highest divergence). What changes overwhelmingly is soft-clipping: by D=0.10 nearly two-thirds of reads have a divergent end clipped off. The clipped bases are exactly the ones carrying alternate alleles, so clipping removes alt evidence near read ends — but, as the mechanism and caller sections below show, bwa+GATK still recover most sites, and the dominant loss is downstream in the caller, not here in placement.

3 Reference bias in variant calling

3.1 Fate of true divergence sites

Every truth divergence site is homozygous-alternate and should be called homozygous-alt. The stacked bars show what actually happens. The growing dark band is div_ref_or_absent — sites where the divergent allele is lost and the sample looks like the reference.

div_classes <- c("div_tp","div_het","div_ref_or_absent","div_other")
div_labels  <- c("Recovered (hom-alt)","Called het",
                 "Lost to reference","Other/wrong allele")

div_long <- vcf %>%
  filter(divergence > 0) %>%                       # no divergence sites at D=0
  select(divergence, n_truth_div, all_of(div_classes)) %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(div_classes), names_to = "class", values_to = "n") %>%
  mutate(prop = n / n_truth_div,
         class = factor(class, levels = rev(div_classes)))

dcols <- c("div_tp"="#009e73","div_het"="#56b4e9",
           "div_ref_or_absent"="#d55e00","div_other"="#999999")

ggplot(div_long, aes(x = divergence, y = prop, fill = class)) +
  geom_col(position = position_fill(reverse = TRUE), width = 0.015) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(div_long$divergence)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = dcols,
                    breaks = div_classes, labels = div_labels) +
  xlab("Simulated divergence (D)") + ylab("Proportion of true divergence sites") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

3.2 The headline: divergence lost to the reference

This is the core reference-bias measurement — the fraction of true fixed differences that are called as reference (or not called at all) — plotted against divergence.

bias <- vcf_raw %>%
  filter(divergence > 0) %>%
  mutate(lost_rate = div_ref_or_absent / n_truth_div) %>%
  group_by(divergence) %>%
  summarize(mean = mean(lost_rate), sd = sd(lost_rate), .groups = "drop")

col5 <- corecol(pal="wilke", numcol=1, offset=5)
ggplot(bias, aes(x = divergence, y = mean)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2, color = col5) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd), width = 0.003, color = col5) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = col5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(mean, accuracy = 0.1)), vjust = -1.6, size = 3.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = bias$divergence) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.5)) +
  xlab("Simulated divergence (D)") +
  ylab("Fraction of true SNP divergence sites\ncalled as reference (lost)") +
  bartheme()

Interpretation. Reference bias in SNP calling scales steeply and super-linearly with divergence: ~3% of fixed differences are lost at 2% divergence, rising to ~41% at 10% divergence (error bars are tiny — the three seeds agree closely). At those sites the diverged sample is genotyped as identical to the reference — the empirical phenomenon these simulations were built to quantify, now measured against clean truth. Note this is higher than an equivalent SNP-only genome (~30% at D=0.10): the indels the sample also carries degrade nearby SNP recovery, so ignoring indels would understate reference bias.

4 Heterozygosity recovery

Heterozygosity is held constant at 0.5% across the sweep, yet recovery of het sites degrades as the surrounding divergence increases: het sites embedded in more-divergent sequence increasingly drop out (called reference), so heterozygosity is progressively underestimated the more the sample differs from the reference.

het <- vcf %>%
  mutate(het_tp_rate = het_tp / n_truth_het,
         het_lost_rate = het_ref_or_absent / n_truth_het)

ggplot(het, aes(x = divergence)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = het_tp_rate, color = "Recovered (called het)"), size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = het_tp_rate, color = "Recovered (called het)"), size = 3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = het_lost_rate, color = "Lost to reference"), size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = het_lost_rate, color = "Lost to reference"), size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = het$divergence) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Recovered (called het)" = "#009e73",
                                "Lost to reference" = "#d55e00")) +
  xlab("Simulated divergence (D)") +
  ylab("Fraction of true heterozygous sites") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

5 Reference bias: SNPs vs. indels

Because the sample genome carries both SNPs and small indels, we can ask directly whether indels suffer more reference bias than SNPs — the mechanistic expectation (a read carrying a non-reference indel must be placed with a gap, which aligners penalize far more heavily than a mismatch). Both curves are the fraction of fixed (homozygous) differences that were called as reference, averaged over the three seeds.

lost_by_type <- vcf_raw %>%
  filter(divergence > 0) %>%
  mutate(SNP   = div_ref_or_absent / n_truth_div,
         Indel = indel_div_ref_or_absent / n_truth_indel_div) %>%
  select(divergence, seed, SNP, Indel) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(SNP, Indel), names_to = "type", values_to = "lost") %>%
  group_by(divergence, type) %>%
  summarize(mean = mean(lost), sd = sd(lost), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(lost_by_type, aes(x = divergence, y = mean, color = type)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd), width = 0.003) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(lost_by_type$divergence)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.55)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("SNP" = "#0072b2", "Indel" = "#d55e00")) +
  xlab("Simulated divergence (D)") +
  ylab("Fixed differences called as reference (lost)") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Interpretation. Indels are lost to the reference at a higher rate than SNPs at every divergence level — from ~1.8× worse at low divergence (5.5% vs 3.0% at D=0.02) to ~1.15× worse at high divergence (47.6% vs 41.2% at D=0.10). This confirms, in our own controlled measurement, the expectation that reference bias is stronger around indels; the gap is proportionally largest when divergence is low, exactly where a single indel stands out most against otherwise reference-matching sequence.

het_by_type <- vcf_raw %>%
  mutate(SNP   = het_tp / n_truth_het,
         Indel = indel_het_tp / n_truth_indel_het) %>%
  select(divergence, seed, SNP, Indel) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(SNP, Indel), names_to = "type", values_to = "rec") %>%
  group_by(divergence, type) %>%
  summarize(mean = mean(rec), sd = sd(rec), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(het_by_type, aes(x = divergence, y = mean, color = type)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd), width = 0.003) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(het_by_type$divergence)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("SNP" = "#0072b2", "Indel" = "#d55e00")) +
  xlab("Simulated divergence (D)") +
  ylab("Heterozygous sites correctly called het") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Interpretation. Heterozygous indels are also recovered less well than heterozygous SNPs across the whole range (e.g. 45% vs 56% at D=0.10), so the underestimation of within-sample variation under reference bias is worse for indels than for SNPs.

6 False positives

False positives (positions called variant that are not truth sites) remain a small fraction of calls, but rise with divergence — a secondary effect of mismapped, allele-mismatched reads accumulating in more-divergent simulations.

fp <- vcf %>% mutate(fp_rate = fp / n_called_snp)

p_fp_n <- ggplot(fp, aes(x = divergence, y = fp)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.1, color = corecol(pal="wilke", numcol=1, offset=1)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = corecol(pal="wilke", numcol=1, offset=1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = fp$divergence) +
  xlab("Divergence (D)") + ylab("False positive SNPs (count)") + bartheme()

p_fp_r <- ggplot(fp, aes(x = divergence, y = fp_rate)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.1, color = corecol(pal="wilke", numcol=1, offset=1)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = corecol(pal="wilke", numcol=1, offset=1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = fp$divergence) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  xlab("Divergence (D)") + ylab("FP as fraction of called SNPs") + bartheme()

plot_grid(p_fp_n, p_fp_r, ncol = 2, labels = c("Count","Rate"))

7 Mechanism: why are divergence sites lost?

Data note: this section uses the earlier SNP-only replicate (seed 42), which is why its SNP loss rates run slightly lower than the SNP+indel results above. The mechanism it isolates — the shift from mapping-limited to caller-limited loss with divergence — is the point here and is unaffected.

The variant-calling section shows divergence sites increasingly called as reference, but not why. To pin down the mechanism without the divergence confound, we take a per-site view at each divergence level: every truth divergence site is homozygous-alternate, so every read that truly covers it (known exactly from the mason truth BAM) should carry the ALT allele. We trace each such read to its fate in the mapped BAM and compare recovered sites (div_tp) against lost sites (div_ref_or_absent) at the same divergence.

Sampling / definitions. Up to 10,000 sites per outcome class per divergence were randomly sampled (seed 42); D=0.00 has no divergence sites and is omitted. A read’s fate is retained (aligned across the site, showing ALT / REF / other base), soft-clipped over the site, mismapped (>150 bp from truth), or unmapped. The “effective ALT fraction” counts only MAPQ ≥ 20 reads — the reads GATK HaplotypeCaller actually uses — so sites lost to low mapping quality are separated from sites lost to read dropout. See summary-data/mm39-mason-chr19-site-linkage.csv.dict.txt for full field definitions.

link <- read_csv("summary-data/mm39-mason-chr19-site-linkage.csv")

fate_cols <- c("retained_alt","retained_ref","clipped","mismapped","unmapped")
fate_labs <- c("Aligned, ALT (support kept)","Aligned, REF (seq error)",
               "Soft-clipped over site","Mismapped (>150bp)","Unmapped")

# Fraction of truly-covering reads in each fate, weighted by site depth,
# split by call outcome and divergence.
fate_summ <- link %>%
  group_by(divergence, outcome) %>%
  summarize(truth = sum(truth_depth),
            across(all_of(fate_cols), sum), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(fate_cols), ~ .x / truth)) %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(fate_cols), names_to = "fate", values_to = "frac") %>%
  mutate(fate = factor(fate, levels = fate_cols),
         outcome = factor(outcome, levels = c("tp","lost"),
                          labels = c("Recovered (div_tp)","Lost to reference")))

fcols <- c("retained_alt"="#009e73","retained_ref"="#999999",
           "clipped"="#e69f00","mismapped"="#d55e00","unmapped"="#000000")

ggplot(fate_summ, aes(x = divergence, y = frac, fill = fate)) +
  geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE), width = 0.015) +
  facet_wrap(~outcome) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = fcols, breaks = fate_cols, labels = fate_labs) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0,0)) +
  xlab("Simulated divergence (D)") + ylab("Fraction of truly-covering reads") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Interpretation. Recovered sites keep almost all reads aligned with ALT support at every divergence. Lost sites lose reads by two different routes: mismapping dominates at low divergence (repetitive regions), while soft-clipping over the site grows with divergence. But note both effects are partial — even lost sites keep most of their alt-bearing reads.

7.1 Effective alternate-allele fraction the caller sees

If read dropout were the whole story, lost sites would show a depressed ALT fraction. This plots the effective ALT fraction (MAPQ ≥ 20 reads) for recovered vs. lost sites.

vaf <- link %>%
  group_by(divergence, outcome) %>%
  summarize(alt_hq = sum(pileup_alt_hq), depth_hq = sum(pileup_depth_hq),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(alt_frac_hq = alt_hq / depth_hq,
         outcome = factor(outcome, levels = c("tp","lost"),
                          labels = c("Recovered","Lost")))

ggplot(vaf, aes(x = divergence, y = alt_frac_hq, color = outcome)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2) + geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Recovered"="#009e73","Lost"="#d55e00")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0,1)) +
  xlab("Simulated divergence (D)") +
  ylab("Effective ALT fraction\n(MAPQ >= 20 reads at the site)") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Interpretation. At low divergence the lost sites really do have a depressed ALT fraction (~71% at D=0.02) — read mapping explains the loss. But as divergence rises, the ALT fraction at lost sites climbs back to ~94%, nearly as high as recovered sites. That means at high divergence most lost sites have clean, high-confidence alternate evidence and still are not called — read mapping no longer explains the loss.

7.2 Two mechanisms, shifting with divergence

Classifying each lost site by whether its alternate evidence was actually degraded (effective ALT fraction < 50%, a read-mapping failure) or was present but uncalled (≥ 50%, a caller/region-complexity failure) shows the balance tip with divergence.

VAF_CUT <- 0.5   # heuristic: a hom-alt site with >=50% MAPQ>=20 ALT should be callable
cause <- link %>%
  filter(outcome == "lost") %>%
  mutate(cause = ifelse(pileup_alt_frac_hq < VAF_CUT,
                        "Read evidence lost (ALT frac < 50%)",
                        "Evidence present, not called (ALT frac >= 50%)")) %>%
  group_by(divergence, cause) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(divergence) %>%
  mutate(frac = n / sum(n))

ccols <- c("Read evidence lost (ALT frac < 50%)"="#d55e00",
           "Evidence present, not called (ALT frac >= 50%)"="#56b4e9")

ggplot(cause, aes(x = divergence, y = frac, fill = cause)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.015) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = ccols) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = c(0,0)) +
  xlab("Simulated divergence (D)") +
  ylab("Fraction of lost divergence sites") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Interpretation & takeaway. Reference bias in the calls has two mechanisms whose balance shifts with divergence:

  • Low divergence — mapping-limited. Lost sites are concentrated in repetitive regions where alt-bearing reads mismap, depressing the alternate fraction below the callable range.
  • High divergence — caller-limited. Reads still carry the alternate allele with high MAPQ, yet the sites are lost. This is not mainly about soft-clipping (which rises with divergence but affects recovered sites too) — it is a property of GATK HaplotypeCaller’s local reassembly step (see the caller-swap test below).

7.3 What the losses actually are: density vs. caller

Two direct checks pin this down.

Local variant density only weakly distinguishes lost from recovered sites: the median distance to the nearest other variant is just 1–2 bp smaller at lost sites (e.g. 3 vs 4 bp at D=0.10), and at high divergence ~99% of all sites have a neighbour within 20 bp. So “dense region” is not a clean explanation — an earlier draft overstated it.

Swapping the caller is decisive. Re-calling the D=0.10 BAM with a pileup-based caller (bcftools, which does no local reassembly) recovers the GATK-lost sites by outcome class:

GATK site class bcftools recovers
recovered by GATK (sanity check) 99.2%
GATK-lost, evidence degraded (ALT frac < 50%) 0.6%
GATK-lost, evidence present (ALT frac ≥ 50%) 98.7%

So the large “evidence present but uncalled” class is ~99% recoverable simply by using a non-assembly caller — the loss is specific to HaplotypeCaller’s assembly, not a lack of evidence. The “evidence degraded” (mapping-limited) sites are recovered by neither caller, as expected — those need better mapping, not a better caller.

Caveats: the caller-swap is one condition (D=0.10, one seed) and measures recall only — bcftools’ false-positive rate at high divergence has not yet been checked, so “more robust” is provisional pending a precision comparison. The 50% ALT-fraction cutoff separating the two lost classes is a heuristic.

7.4 Decomposition: which mechanism drives the loss?

Putting it together — the overall SNP loss rate split into its two mechanisms as a fraction of all true divergence sites. Each cell is how much of the genome’s fixed SNP differences are lost to that mechanism at that divergence.

decomp <- read_csv("summary-data/mm39-mason-chr19-loss-decomposition.csv") %>%
  mutate(mechanism = factor(mechanism, levels = c("mapping-limited", "caller-limited")))

ggplot(decomp, aes(x = factor(divergence), y = mechanism, fill = frac_of_truth_lost)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", size = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(frac_of_truth_lost, accuracy = 0.1)), size = 3.4) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f7f7f7", high = "#d55e00",
                      labels = scales::percent,
                      name = "Fraction of true\nSNP sites lost") +
  xlab("Simulated divergence (D)") + ylab("Loss mechanism") +
  bartheme() +
  theme(legend.position = "right", axis.line = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank())

Interpretation. The two mechanisms behave completely differently. Mapping-limited loss is a small, nearly flat floor (~0.6% → 1.4% across the whole divergence range) — essentially the fixed repetitive fraction of the chromosome, where alt reads mismap no matter what. Caller-limited loss explodes (1.6% → 28%) and accounts for almost all of the growth in reference bias. So as divergence rises, the reference-bias problem is overwhelmingly the assembly-based caller failing on sites whose evidence is present — which is why it also resolves the earlier puzzle: mapping-limited loss barely changes in absolute terms, so its share of all lost sites shrinks even as more reads mismap. It also says where effort pays off: at realistic divergences, a better/pileup caller (or iterative mapping that lowers effective divergence) addresses the dominant term, while graph/iterative mapping chips at the small mapping-limited floor.

8 Variant caller benchmark

The mechanism section showed the high-divergence SNP loss is specific to GATK HaplotypeCaller’s assembly. Here we test that comprehensively: holding mapping fixed (the same bwa BAMs), we call variants with three callers spanning the strategy axis — gatk (reference-anchored De Bruijn assembly), bcftools (pileup, no assembly), and freebayes (haplotype-from-alignment, no k-mer reassembly) — and score each caller’s recall and precision across the divergence sweep. All callers use their native output normalized identically (bcftools norm -m- --atomize), so precision reflects each caller’s intrinsic false-positive tradeoff.

cb <- read_csv("summary-data/mm39-mason-chr19-caller-benchmark.csv") %>%
  mutate(caller = factor(caller, levels = c("gatk", "bcftools", "freebayes")))

cb_m <- cb %>% group_by(caller, divergence) %>%
  summarize(snp_recall    = mean(div_tp / n_truth_div),
            snp_precision  = mean(1 - fp / n_called_snp),
            indel_recall   = mean(indel_div_tp / n_truth_indel_div),
            .groups = "drop")

# heatmap helper: caller (y) x divergence (x), fill = metric
caller_heatmap <- function(df, metric, name, high) {
  ggplot(df, aes(x = factor(divergence), y = caller, fill = .data[[metric]])) +
    geom_tile(color = "white", size = 0.6) +
    geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(.data[[metric]], accuracy = 1)), size = 3.2) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f7f7f7", high = high, labels = scales::percent,
                        limits = c(0, 1), name = name) +
    xlab("Divergence (D)") + ylab(NULL) + bartheme() +
    theme(axis.line = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
          legend.position = "right")
}

8.1 SNP recall and precision

r <- caller_heatmap(filter(cb_m, divergence > 0), "snp_recall", "SNP\nrecall", "#0072b2")
p <- caller_heatmap(cb_m, "snp_precision", "SNP\nprecision", "#009e73")
cowplot::plot_grid(r, p, ncol = 1, labels = c("SNP recall (divergence sites)", "SNP precision"),
                   label_size = 11, hjust = 0)

Interpretation. For SNPs, both non-assembly callers dramatically out-recall GATK as divergence rises — at D=0.10, GATK recovers only 58% of fixed SNP differences vs 86% (bcftools) and 84% (freebayes). But the precision panel shows the catch: bcftools keeps GATK-level precision (~97%), while freebayes’ precision collapses to ~84% (one in six of its calls is a false positive at D=0.10). So for SNPs at high divergence, bcftools is the clear win — large recall gain at essentially no precision cost — whereas freebayes buys recall with a heavy false-positive penalty.

8.2 Indels — the tradeoff reverses

caller_heatmap(filter(cb_m, divergence > 0), "indel_recall", "Indel\nrecall", "#d55e00")

Interpretation. For indels the ranking flips: bcftools collapses (indel recall falls to ~4% at D=0.10), while GATK and freebayes retain ~45%. Pileup calling is intrinsically weak at indels — and worse in divergent, complex regions — whereas the assembly (GATK) and haplotype-from-alignment (freebayes) strategies reconstruct indels far better. So the very assembly/haplotype machinery that hurts GATK on divergent SNPs is what indels need.

8.3 Recall and precision vs divergence

Divergence on the x-axis, one line per caller, split into recall vs precision (rows) and SNP vs indel (columns). This is the at-a-glance view: read each panel left-to-right to see how that metric holds up (or doesn’t) as the sample diverges from the reference.

metrics_long <- cb %>% group_by(caller, divergence) %>%
  summarize(`SNP recall`     = mean(div_tp / n_truth_div),
            `SNP precision`   = mean(1 - fp / n_called_snp),
            `indel recall`    = mean(indel_div_tp / n_truth_indel_div),
            `indel precision` = mean(ifelse(n_called_indel > 0, 1 - fp_indel / n_called_indel, NA)),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_longer(-c(caller, divergence), names_to = "panel", values_to = "value") %>%
  separate(panel, into = c("variant", "metric"), sep = " ") %>%
  filter(!is.nan(value), !is.na(value))       # recall undefined at D=0

metrics_long$variant <- factor(metrics_long$variant, levels = c("SNP", "indel"))
metrics_long$metric  <- factor(metrics_long$metric,  levels = c("recall", "precision"))

ggplot(metrics_long, aes(x = divergence, y = value, color = caller)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.1) + geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  facet_grid(metric ~ variant) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(metrics_long$divergence)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(gatk = "#d55e00", bcftools = "#0072b2", freebayes = "#009e73")) +
  labs(x = "Simulated divergence (D)", y = NULL) +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Reading it. Top row (recall): for SNPs, GATK falls away steeply while bcftools and freebayes stay high; for indels, bcftools falls off a cliff while GATK and freebayes decline gently together. Bottom row (precision): GATK and bcftools hold high precision for SNPs while freebayes drifts down. Same four numbers as the heatmaps, but the divergence trend is immediate.

8.4 Precision–recall trajectories (all methods in one view)

The same data as a precision–recall plot: each caller is a path through PR space, one point per divergence level, the arrow pointing toward increasing divergence. Top-right is the ideal (high recall and precision); a method that degrades gracefully stays near the top-right, one that trades recall or precision away slides left or down.

pr <- cb %>% group_by(caller, divergence) %>%
  summarize(SNP_recall      = mean(div_tp / n_truth_div),
            SNP_precision    = mean(1 - fp / n_called_snp),
            indel_recall     = mean(indel_div_tp / n_truth_indel_div),
            indel_precision  = mean(ifelse(n_called_indel > 0, 1 - fp_indel / n_called_indel, NA)),
            .groups = "drop")

prl <- bind_rows(
  pr %>% transmute(caller, divergence, variant = "SNP",
                   recall = SNP_recall, precision = SNP_precision),
  pr %>% transmute(caller, divergence, variant = "indel",
                   recall = indel_recall, precision = indel_precision)
) %>% filter(divergence > 0) %>%           # recall undefined at D=0
  arrange(caller, variant, divergence)     # path order = increasing divergence

prl$variant <- factor(prl$variant, levels = c("SNP", "indel"))

ggplot(prl, aes(x = recall, y = precision, color = caller, group = caller)) +
  geom_path(arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm"), type = "closed"), size = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(size = as.numeric(divergence))) +
  facet_wrap(~variant) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(gatk = "#d55e00", bcftools = "#0072b2", freebayes = "#009e73")) +
  scale_size_continuous(name = "Divergence", range = c(1.5, 5)) +
  labs(x = "Recall", y = "Precision") +
  bartheme() + theme(legend.position = "right")

Reading it. SNP panel: bcftools (blue) stays pinned to the top-right — recall erodes only slightly and precision holds — while GATK (orange) slides straight left (recall collapses, precision intact) and freebayes (green) sags down-and-left (losing both). Indel panel: the picture inverts — GATK and freebayes stay upper/right-ish while bcftools shoots to the far left (indel recall → ~0). One figure captures the whole story: which method to trust depends on the variant type and how much precision vs recall you can spend.

Takeaway. There is no single best caller across the board:

  • SNPs at high divergence: bcftools (best recall and precision).
  • Indels: GATK or freebayes (bcftools fails); freebayes matches GATK’s indel recall.
  • freebayes overall: strong recall for both types but a real SNP precision cost.

This reframes “reference bias is a caller problem” precisely: it’s a caller problem for SNPs, fixable by dropping the assembly requirement — but indels genuinely need haplotype/assembly reconstruction, so the lever there is better mapping (graph or iterative, to lower effective divergence) rather than a simpler caller.

Caveats: native (unfiltered) calls, so GATK’s numbers here differ from the filtered main-results section; chr19, single iteration, 3 seeds; freebayes’ complex alleles are atomized to compare fairly.

9 Summary

  • The v1 liftover artifact is gone: missing reads = 0 at every divergence level, so these numbers are trustworthy.
  • Mapping is robust to divergence at the read level: reads land at the right locus (mismapping <2%, unmapped dropout only at 8–10%). The big change is soft-clipping (up to 62% of reads at D=0.10); a whole-read positional shift stays negligible (~2%).
  • Reference bias lives in variant calling: the fraction of true fixed SNP differences called as reference rises from ~3% (D=0.02) to ~41% (D=0.10), tight across the three seeds.
  • Indels suffer more than SNPs: fixed indels are lost to the reference at a higher rate than SNPs at every divergence (up to ~1.8× at low D), and het indels are recovered less well than het SNPs — reference bias is stronger around indels.
  • Indels worsen SNP recovery too: SNP loss is higher here than in a SNP-only genome (~41% vs ~30% at D=0.10), so ignoring indels understates reference bias.
  • Heterozygosity is underestimated more as divergence grows, despite a constant simulated het rate; the effect is larger for indels.
  • Two mechanisms, shifting with divergence (mechanism section): mapping-limited loss (repeats/mismapping) dominates at low divergence; at high divergence the loss is caller-specific — a pileup caller recovers the high-evidence sites GATK’s assembler drops.
  • Caller benchmark (mapping fixed): for SNPs at D=0.10, GATK recovers 58% vs bcftools 86% at matched precision (freebayes 84% but precision drops to ~84%). For indels the ranking reverses — bcftools collapses (~4%), GATK/freebayes retain ~45%. So reference bias is a caller problem for SNPs (drop the assembly requirement); indels need haplotype/assembly reconstruction, i.e. better mapping.
  • False positives stay low for GATK/bcftools (<0.3% of calls) but increase with divergence; freebayes is markedly more FP-prone at high divergence.

Scope: single chromosome (chr19), chr19-only mapping, 3 replicate seeds, single iteration. Whole-genome mapping, a v1-vs-v2 comparison, and iterative (pseudo-it) mapping are planned extensions.
